title: The Dangers and the Debates
summary: Rockets are amazing, but they can also be dangerous. Brave astronauts have been lost, rockets have been used as weapons, and old bits of satellites now zoom around Earth like a swarm of tiny bullets. In this part we look at the hard questions: how do we keep people safe, keep space clean, and make sure space is fair for everyone?

sections.heading: The Price of Reaching Up
paragraphs: Every story about rockets has a quiet side. When you read about countdowns, fire and cheering crowds, it is easy to forget that a rocket is really a controlled explosion with people sitting on top of it. Space does not care how brave or clever you are, and one small mistake can be enough. Over the decades, some of the bravest people of their time paid for that lesson with their lives. Remembering them is part of telling the story honestly.

The first big loss of the American program did not even happen in space. On 27 January 1967, the Apollo 1 crew, Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee, were strapped into their capsule on Launch Complex 34 in Florida for a practice countdown. The cabin was filled with pure oxygen at slightly more than normal air pressure, which makes almost anything burn fiercely. A spark, probably from damaged wiring, started a fire that spread in seconds. The hatch opened inwards and was held shut by the pressure inside, so the crew could not escape in time. All three died.

NASA was shaken, and the whole Apollo spacecraft was redesigned. The new hatch could swing outward in a few seconds. Flammable materials were replaced. On the launch pad, the cabin air became a mix of nitrogen and oxygen instead of pure oxygen. Many astronauts later said that Apollo would never have reached the Moon safely without the hard changes made after the fire.

Only three months later, on 24 April 1967, the Soviet cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov was coming home in Soyuz 1, a brand-new spacecraft that had many problems from the moment it reached orbit. During the descent, the main parachute did not come out of its container, and the reserve parachute tangled. The capsule hit the ground at high speed and Komarov was killed. He was the first person to die during a space mission.

In June 1971 came an even stranger tragedy. Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev had just spent more than three weeks aboard Salyut 1, the world's first space station. As their Soyuz 11 capsule separated from the rest of the spacecraft on the way home, a small valve was jolted open. The cabin air leaked away into space in a short time. The three men were not wearing pressure suits, because the cramped capsule had been designed without room for them. When the recovery team opened the hatch after landing, the crew was gone. Because their deaths happened above the Kármán line, these three cosmonauts are the only people known to have died in space itself. After Soyuz 11, every Soviet and Russian crew wore pressure suits during launch and landing, and they still do.

The American Space Shuttle program had two disasters. On 28 January 1986, on a very cold Florida morning, Challenger lifted off. A rubber seal called an O-ring, in a joint of the right solid rocket booster, had stiffened in the cold and did not seal properly. Hot gas escaped through the joint, and about 73 seconds after launch the external tank came apart and Challenger broke up in the sky. The seven people aboard died, including Christa McAuliffe, a schoolteacher who had planned to teach lessons from orbit. During the investigation, the physicist Richard Feynman dropped a piece of O-ring material into a glass of ice water at a public hearing to show how it lost its springiness in the cold. It was a simple, unforgettable experiment.

On 1 February 2003, Columbia was returning from a 16-day science mission. During its launch, a piece of foam insulation about the size of a small suitcase had broken off the external tank and smashed into the front edge of the left wing, making a hole in the heat protection. Nobody realised how serious the damage was. As Columbia plunged back into the atmosphere, superhot gas entered the wing, and the orbiter broke apart over Texas, only about 16 minutes before it was due to land. Its seven crew members died, including Kalpana Chawla and Ilan Ramon.

Counting the people aboard Soyuz 1, Soyuz 11, Challenger and Columbia, 18 people have died during spaceflight missions. Others died in training. In March 1961, a young cosmonaut trainee named Valentin Bondarenko died after a fire in a pressure chamber filled with oxygen, an accident the Soviet Union kept secret for many years; the full story only came out in the 1980s. In 2014, the test pilot Michael Alsbury was killed when Virgin Galactic's rocket plane VSS Enterprise broke apart during a test flight over California's Mojave Desert, while his fellow pilot Peter Siebold survived. Every one of these losses led to investigations, new rules and safer machines. That is how the people who were lost still protect astronauts today.

sections.heading: Disasters on the Ground
paragraphs: Some of the worst rocket accidents never left the launch pad. The deadliest is known as the Nedelin catastrophe. On 24 October 1960, at the secret Soviet launch base now called Baikonur, in what is today Kazakhstan, engineers were rushing to prepare the first test of a new missile called the R-16. It was meant to be an intercontinental ballistic missile, a rocket weapon that could carry a nuclear bomb across the world. Its fuels were toxic chemicals that burst into flame the instant they touched each other, which made them convenient for a weapon but dangerous for the people working around it.

There was great pressure to launch quickly, before an important national holiday in November. A fault in the electrical system made the second-stage engine fire while the rocket was still standing on the pad, full of fuel and surrounded by people. The rocket exploded into a huge fireball. The commander of the Soviet missile forces, Chief Marshal Mitrofan Nedelin, was among those killed. The exact number of deaths is still uncertain: an official investigation in the 1990s counted 78, while other estimates range from about 50 to more than 120. The chief designer of the missile, Mikhail Yangel, survived only because he had stepped away behind a protective bunker moments before.

The Soviet government hid the disaster. The public was told that Nedelin had died in a plane crash, and families were told to say the same. The truth was not officially admitted until 1989, almost 30 years later. Secrecy like this was common on both sides of the Cold War, and it meant that hard lessons were sometimes learned slowly.

Today, launch sites are built very differently. Workers watch launches from blast-proof control rooms far away. Before liftoff, the area is cleared for kilometres around. Many rockets carry a range safety system, which can destroy a rocket that flies off course before it threatens a town. Rockets that carry people often have a launch escape system, a small, very powerful rocket that can yank the crew capsule away from a failing booster. This has already saved lives. In September 1983, a fire broke out at the base of a Soyuz rocket on the pad, and the escape tower pulled cosmonauts Vladimir Titov and Gennady Strekalov to safety seconds before the rocket exploded. In October 2018, a booster failed during the launch of Soyuz MS-10, and the capsule carrying Alexey Ovchinin and NASA's Nick Hague separated automatically and landed safely in Kazakhstan. Both men flew to space again a few months later.

sections.heading: From Weapons to Treaties
paragraphs: Throughout this Deep Dive, rockets have had two faces. The same push that lifts a spacecraft can carry a bomb. From the fire arrows of China to Tipu Sultan's iron rockets and the V-2, rockets were weapons long before they were spaceships. Even the rocket that launched Sputnik, the R-7, was first built to carry a nuclear warhead to the other side of the world.

During the Cold War, the United States and the Soviet Union built thousands of intercontinental ballistic missiles, or ICBMs. An ICBM goes up into space and comes back down on a target thousands of kilometres away, about 30 minutes after launch. In October 1962, during the Cuban Missile Crisis, the world came frighteningly close to nuclear war over Soviet missiles placed in Cuba. People everywhere realised that rocket technology had made the whole planet vulnerable.

Then came the most important space law ever written. The Outer Space Treaty was opened for signing on 27 January 1967 and came into force in October that year. Today more than 100 countries have joined it, including every country that launches people into space. Its main rules are simple and remarkable. No country may place nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit, on the Moon or anywhere else in space. The Moon and other worlds may be used only for peaceful purposes, with no military bases or weapons tests there. No country can claim the Moon, a planet or any part of them as its own territory. Countries are responsible for whatever their companies and citizens do in space, and they must pay if their spacecraft cause damage. Astronauts are called envoys of all humankind, and any country must help them if they are in trouble.

The treaty did not answer every question. A later agreement, the Moon Agreement of 1979, tried to say that the Moon's resources belong to everyone, but only a small number of countries joined it, and none of the biggest space powers did. Since 2020, many countries have signed the Artemis Accords, a set of principles led by the United States about peaceful exploration, sharing scientific data and using resources such as lunar ice. By late 2026, more than 75 countries had signed. China and Russia have not, and are planning their own lunar research station together. People still argue about whether mining the Moon or asteroids is fair, and who should decide. These are not just questions for lawyers: whoever grows up to explore the Moon may have to live by the answers.

sections.heading: A Junkyard in the Sky
paragraphs: Look up on a clear night and the sky seems empty and calm. In fact, the space just above our atmosphere is getting crowded. Besides thousands of working satellites, there are dead satellites, empty rocket stages, lost tools, flakes of paint and countless fragments from explosions and crashes. All of this is called space debris, or space junk.

Space agencies keep careful track of it. NASA says the US Space Surveillance Network routinely follows objects larger than about 10 cm, about the size of a softball, and that there are tens of thousands of these large, trackable objects. Below that size, the numbers explode. Scientists estimate there are around a million pieces between 1 and 10 cm across, and about 100 million pieces around a millimetre in size, far too small to track one by one.

Why worry about a speck the size of a grain of sand? Because of speed. In low Earth orbit, debris travels at about 7 to 8 km per second, many times faster than a bullet. When two objects meet, they can hit each other at an average of about 10 km per second. At that speed, even a tiny piece carries a startling amount of energy. In 1983, a fleck of paint smaller than a millimetre left a little crater in a window of the Space Shuttle Challenger, and over the Shuttle program dozens of windows had to be replaced because of such hits. The International Space Station has thick bumper shields on its outside, and it has fired its engines dozens of times since 1999 to dodge larger pieces of junk. Sometimes, when a warning comes too late, the crew climbs into their spacecraft, ready to leave quickly if the station is hit.

The first accidental crash between two whole satellites happened on 10 February 2009, about 790 km above Siberia. Iridium 33, a working American communications satellite, and Cosmos 2251, a dead Russian military satellite that had been switched off for years, slammed into each other at about 11.7 km per second. Both were smashed to pieces, creating about 2,000 trackable fragments and many more smaller ones. Many of those pieces are still circling Earth today.

Some debris was made on purpose. On 11 January 2007, China tested an anti-satellite weapon by launching a missile that smashed into one of its own old weather satellites, Fengyun-1C, about 865 km up. It created more than 3,000 trackable pieces, the largest single debris-making event ever recorded, and because that orbit is so high, much of the debris will stay there for decades or longer. The United States, Russia and India have also destroyed satellites in tests. On 15 November 2021, a Russian missile destroyed an old satellite called Kosmos 1408, creating about 1,500 tracked pieces, and the crew of the space station had to shelter in their spacecraft for safety.

The scariest idea about space junk has a name. In 1978, two NASA scientists, Donald Kessler and Burton Cour-Palais, published a paper warning that if enough objects crowd into one region of orbit, collisions will create fragments, those fragments will cause more collisions, and those will create even more fragments, like a chain reaction. This is now called the Kessler syndrome. In the worst case, some orbits could become so cluttered that they would be too risky to use for a very long time. Scientists disagree about how close we are to that point, but nearly all agree that we must stop making the problem worse.

Some solutions are already in place. Many countries now ask satellite operators to bring old satellites down so they burn up in the atmosphere, instead of leaving them in orbit. In 2022, the US Federal Communications Commission set a rule that US-licensed satellites in low orbit should come down within five years of the end of their mission. Rocket stages are designed to vent leftover fuel so they do not explode later. Engineers are also testing ways to clean up junk: in 2024, a Japanese spacecraft called ADRAS-J, built by the company Astroscale, flew close to an old rocket stage and photographed it, practising the first step toward one day grabbing it and pulling it down.

sections.heading: Rockets and the Planet
paragraphs: Compared with cars, planes and power stations, rockets burn only a small amount of fuel in total, and their share of the world's greenhouse gas emissions is tiny. So why do scientists study their effect on the environment? Because rockets release their exhaust in places nothing else reaches, and because the number of launches is growing quickly.

Different fuels make different exhaust. Engines that burn hydrogen and oxygen produce mostly water vapour, though making the hydrogen on Earth uses a lot of energy. Kerosene engines, like those on the Saturn V and many modern rockets, also release soot, tiny black particles of carbon. Solid rocket boosters release chlorine compounds and fine particles of aluminium oxide. Down near the ground this exhaust is soon washed away. But high up in the stratosphere, more than 10 km above us, there is no rain to clean the air. Particles injected there can float for years. Scientists are studying whether, if launches keep multiplying, soot could warm the stratosphere and chemicals could thin the ozone layer, the shield that protects us from the Sun's ultraviolet light. Right now the effects are small, but researchers want to understand them before they grow.

Launch sites have neighbours too. NASA's Kennedy Space Center in Florida shares its land with the Merritt Island National Wildlife Refuge, home to sea turtles, manatees, alligators and hundreds of kinds of birds. Rocket noise, lights and occasional fires all have to be managed carefully. When the first Starship test flight lifted off from south Texas in April 2023, its engines blasted apart the concrete under the launch mount and scattered chunks and dust across the surrounding area, which included protected wildlife habitat. Some rockets, especially older Russian and Chinese ones, burn toxic fuels, and their empty first stages fall onto land rather than into the ocean, sometimes near farms and villages.

There is also a newer problem, and it shows up on astronomers' photos. Since 2019, companies have launched thousands of small satellites to beam internet service around the world. These huge groups are called megaconstellations. Soon after launch, the satellites can be bright enough to see with the naked eye, sometimes looking like a string of pearls crossing the night. For telescopes that take long-exposure pictures of the sky, each passing satellite can leave a bright streak across the image. Radio telescopes, which listen for faint signals from space, can also be disturbed by satellite radio signals.

Astronomers and satellite companies have started working together. SpaceX tested darker coatings and sunshades to make its satellites dimmer, and astronomers are writing software to spot and remove streaks. In 2022, the International Astronomical Union set up a centre to protect dark and quiet skies. The debate is about balance: satellite internet can connect remote schools, ships and disaster zones, but the night sky is also a treasure that belongs to everyone, and it has inspired people for as long as there have been people.

sections.heading: Is Space Worth the Money?
paragraphs: Spaceflight is expensive. The Apollo program cost about 25.8 billion US dollars at the time, which is roughly 250 billion dollars or more in today's money. In 1966, at the height of the Moon race, NASA's budget was more than 4% of all the money the US federal government spent. Today it is much smaller, about four-tenths of one percent, though it is still many billions of dollars a year. Other countries also spend large sums on rockets, satellites and astronauts. So a fair question has been asked again and again: should this money be spent on problems here on Earth instead?

People were already asking that while Apollo 11 stood on the pad. On 15 July 1969, the day before launch, the civil rights leader Ralph Abernathy led a group of poor families, some with mule-drawn wagons, to the gates of the Kennedy Space Center. He said the money for the Moon could help hungry people in America. NASA's leader Thomas Paine went out to meet him. Paine said that if not pushing the launch button tomorrow would solve the problems Abernathy was talking about, they would not push it, but that space technology was far easier than solving poverty. He invited the group to watch the launch, and Abernathy said he would pray for the astronauts' safety. The two men disagreed, but they treated each other with respect.

What has space work actually given us? Some benefits are huge. The first weather satellite, TIROS-1, sent back pictures of clouds from orbit in April 1960, and today weather satellites give warnings of hurricanes and storms days in advance, saving countless lives. Communication satellites carry television, phone calls and internet. In July 1962, Telstar 1 relayed the first live television pictures across the Atlantic. The Global Positioning System, or GPS, was built by the US military, with the first satellite launched in 1978, and now guides cars, ships, planes and phones everywhere. Its clocks must even be corrected for Einstein's theory of relativity, or positions would drift by kilometres every day.

Smaller inventions came out of space research too. NASA has published a magazine called Spinoff every year since 1976 describing more than 2,000 technologies that started in space work and became products. A tough coating developed at NASA's Ames Research Center was licensed in the 1980s to make scratch-resistant sunglasses and spectacle lenses. Systems developed to keep drinking water clean on spacecraft helped improve water filters. Memory foam came from a 1960s NASA project to make safer aircraft seats. The tiny camera chips in most mobile phones grew out of work at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in the 1990s.

But beware of myths. NASA did not invent Velcro, which was invented by the Swiss engineer George de Mestral in the 1940s. It did not invent Tang, the orange drink powder made by General Foods in the 1950s, or Teflon, discovered by accident at the chemical company DuPont in 1938. Astronauts used them, which made them famous. And the story that NASA spent millions on a space pen while Russian cosmonauts just used pencils is not true: the Fisher Space Pen was developed with private money, and both the American and Soviet programs bought it.

sections.heading: Hidden Figures and Who Gets to Go
paragraphs: Who gets the credit for a rocket? For a long time, history books told the story through a few famous astronauts and engineers. But every launch depends on thousands of people, and some of them were left out of the story for decades because of their sex, their skin colour or the secrecy of their work.

At the Langley laboratory in Hampton, Virginia, starting in the 1940s, teams of women worked as human computers, doing long, careful calculations by hand for aircraft and, later, spacecraft. Because Virginia's laws enforced racial segregation, the Black women mathematicians worked in a separate group called the West Area Computers, and they had to use separate dining areas and bathrooms. Dorothy Vaughan became the group's leader in 1949, the first Black supervisor at the laboratory, and later taught herself and her team the computer language FORTRAN when electronic computers arrived. Mary Jackson became NASA's first Black woman engineer in 1958.

Katherine Johnson calculated flight paths for the Mercury flights and for Apollo. Before John Glenn's orbital flight in 1962, he asked that she personally check the numbers produced by the new electronic computer; he trusted her more than the machine. For years, few people outside NASA knew her name. In 2015, at the age of 97, she received the Presidential Medal of Freedom, and the 2016 book and film Hidden Figures finally told the story of these women to millions of people.

Women who wanted to be astronauts faced closed doors too. In 1960 and 1961, a doctor named William Randolph Lovelace II privately put a group of women pilots, including Jerrie Cobb, through some of the same medical tests given to the Mercury men. Several did very well. But the testing was stopped, and NASA at the time only chose military jet test pilots, a job women were not allowed to do. The group later became known as the Mercury 13. None of them flew in space for NASA. The first American woman in space, Sally Ride, did not fly until 1983, twenty years after the Soviet Union's Valentina Tereshkova. In 2021, one of the Mercury 13, Wally Funk, finally reached space at the age of 82 aboard Blue Origin's New Shepard.

Other hidden workers did not choose their role at all. As Part 7 of this story told, thousands of prisoners were forced to build V-2 rockets in the underground Mittelwerk factory, and many of them died. Their story was barely mentioned for decades while some of the engineers who used their labour became celebrated in America. Today, a memorial at the site of the Mittelbau-Dora camp in Germany helps make sure they are remembered.

There are also questions about who gets to go now. Fewer than a thousand people have ever been to space, and for most of history they were chosen from just a few countries. That is slowly changing: astronauts now come from dozens of nations, and crews include more women and people from many backgrounds. Private spaceflight has opened another door, but it is very expensive. In 2001, the American businessman Dennis Tito paid about 20 million dollars to visit the International Space Station, and tickets for private trips to orbit still cost tens of millions. Some people worry that space could become a playground only for the very rich. Others hope prices will keep falling, just as flying in an aeroplane went from a luxury to something millions of families do.

There are no easy answers to these debates. But the people asking hard questions, from Ralph Abernathy at the gates of the space centre to astronomers counting satellite streaks, have often made spaceflight better, safer and fairer. And despite all the dangers, people around the world are now getting ready to go back to the Moon, and to travel even further than anyone has gone before.

deepDive: How bad is the space debris problem, really? The physics is what makes it alarming. Kinetic energy grows with the square of speed, so an object hitting at 10 km/s carries about 100 times more energy per kilogram than one hitting at 1 km/s. A 1 cm aluminium fragment at orbital collision speeds can release energy comparable to a small car crash, concentrated on a spot the size of a fingertip. Spacecraft protect themselves with Whipple shields, named after astronomer Fred Whipple, who proposed them in the 1940s: a thin outer bumper sits some distance in front of the main wall, so a fragment that hits the bumper shatters and spreads into a cloud of smaller, slower bits that the inner wall can stop. The space station's critical parts can survive hits from debris up to about 1 cm; for larger tracked pieces, it moves out of the way. Whether we are already in a Kessler cascade is debated. Kessler and Cour-Palais argued in 1978 that above a critical density, collisions would eventually produce debris faster than atmospheric drag removes it. Atmospheric drag is the key: below about 400 to 500 km, debris usually falls back within a few years, especially when the Sun is active and the upper atmosphere swells. Above about 800 km, objects can stay up for centuries, which is why the 2007 Fengyun-1C test and the 2009 Iridium-Cosmos crash were so harmful: both happened in that long-lasting region. Many models suggest that some crowded bands near 800 to 1,000 km are already close to, or past, the point where collisions among existing objects alone would keep the debris growing, even if nobody launched anything new. That is why experts emphasise removing a handful of large dead objects, such as old rocket bodies, which are the most likely to create future swarms of fragments. Megaconstellations change the picture: they put many thousands of satellites at lower altitudes, where failures clear more quickly, but they also require constant automated collision avoidance, with each operator performing thousands of manoeuvres. Some researchers argue that the true limit of orbit is not space but coordination: without shared tracking data and agreed rules, the risk rises faster than the number of satellites.
funFact: When pieces of the Skylab space station fell on Western Australia in 1979, the town of Esperance issued NASA a 400 Australian dollar fine for littering, which an American radio host finally paid off in 2009.
